1:
Henry dates the assembly to the feast of trumpets, a day called a sabbath and kept with a holy convocation, and adds why it carried extra weight: on that day the altar had been set up after the return, a mercy still in living memory, so they had likely kept it ever since with more than ordinary solemnity. Wesley reports the same day and remembrance. Clarke makes it the first day of the civil year and places the water gate on the road from the temple to the brook Kidron; Gill calls the street large and commodious, and has the people come with unanimity, zeal and affection. Henry notes that while sacrifice was tied to the temple door, prayer and praise and preaching are as acceptable in one place as another. Ellicott finds the unanimity rather than the number emphatic, counts men, women and children of years of discretion, and observes that Ezra appears here for the first time in the book, having probably spent twelve years at court. Clarke excludes those incapable of instruction, but will not have a mother shut out for a crying child. Gill thinks Ezra read selected passages rather than straight through, and Ellicott has him and his companions choosing passages hour after hour from daylight.

The pulpit draws everyone's comment. Gill reports the Hebrew word as a tower, so called for its height, its form and its size, since it held fourteen men. Clarke takes it for a platform raised so the people could see and hear a man standing above them, calls it the first intimation we have of a pulpit, and will not have it imagined like the tubs set up in churches, where a preacher is nearly as confined as in the stocks. Ellicott keeps the literal tower of wood and puts the fourteen on what is afterwards called a platform beside him; Delitzsch makes it a stage built for the purpose, six on the right and seven on the left, and argues that a name has dropped out of the Hebrew, since it is improbable there was one fewer on one side than the other. Clarke records that the people stood out of respect for the sacred word, and that both survive in church usage. Gill has the blessing a short prayer wholly benedictory, offered so that what followed might come with greater authority. Ellicott describes the double Amen uttered with lifted hands, the faces then bowed to the ground, and points out that the great God is Nehemiah's phrase, Ezra's own words not being reported.

What the Levites did with the law is the most disputed clause. Wesley has them translate the Hebrew into the Chaldee the people now spoke, having lost their language along with much of their religion, and then expound the meaning and apply it to their condition. Ellicott agrees that they expounded the obscurer passages, naturally turning them into the vernacular. Clarke builds the fullest case: seventy years in Babylon had cost the people both the ancient language and the knowledge of their rites, so that they had even forgotten the feast of tabernacles, and the remedy devised here was not only the origin of the Chaldee paraphrases but probably of preaching from a text. He then takes the verse in four steps: they read in the book of the law; reading distinctly means they expanded and dilated the import of every word; giving the sense means they put weight to it and showed the hearers how nearly it concerned them; and the hearers understood, having a taste and perception of the thing read. Delitzsch dissents on the key word: the sense the Rabbis give it, a rendering into the vulgar tongue, cannot be shown to belong to it, nor will he accept a distinct recitation by appointed rules; what he allows is a paraphrastic exposition and application of the law.
9:
Henry accounts for the weeping by what the law does: it works death and speaks terror, shows men their sins and their danger, and thunders a curse against anyone who does not continue in every part of his duty. That the people were wounded by it he takes for a good sign, their hearts being tender as Josiah's had been, and he notes that when some wept all wept, every one seeing himself guilty before God. Delitzsch reaches the same place by asking what was read: sections of Deuteronomy and other parts of the law, chosen to convict them of transgression and of the punishments they had brought on themselves, which so impressed the crowd that they mourned. Clarke says the verse puts beyond doubt that the Tirshatha is Nehemiah, the word being the name of his office; Gill glosses it governor, the post Zerubbabel had held before him. Henry observes that Nehemiah is brought into the chapter here and not before, and reads the exchange carefully: Ezra was glad to see the people so affected, but Nehemiah judged the mourning unseasonable and Ezra concurred, the day being holy and to be kept with joy and praise. Sorrow for sin, Henry adds, must not hinder our joy in God but rather lead us to it.

Ellicott puts the judgment in terms of the calendar: days of high festival were unsuitable for public and, as he puts it, objective sorrow, the Day of Atonement being on its way for that, and the special day of fasting and covenant already in the leaders' plan. What they tell the people to do instead is read generously. Clarke takes eating the fat and drinking the sweet to mean eating and drinking the best they have, and insists on the second half of the command, that while they feed themselves in the fear of the Lord they remember those who cannot feast and send them portions, so that the thanksgiving may be general and the poor rejoice as much as anyone. Wesley gives the same two motions, feasting before the Lord and sending relief to their poor brethren, and grounds the holiness of the day on its being the feast of trumpets and the opening of a month in which so many days of thanksgiving fell.

The sentence about strength is where the voices spend themselves. Clarke is at pains to say what it does not mean: this is no gluttonous and drunken festival, which enervates the body and enfeebles the mind, but a religious feast from which bodies come away stronger and minds quicker and warmer, able to do God's will and to do it cheerfully. Religious joy tempered by dependence on God's help, by meekness and by self-diffidence, he calls a powerful means of strengthening the soul, in which state every duty is practicable and delightful, and he ends on the proverb that a cheerful heart is not only a continual feast but a continual medicine. Ellicott takes the clause back to its words, literally that delight in Jehovah is a strong refuge, and allows that the beautiful sentence is capable of unlimited application in preaching and devotion. Wesley makes the strength practical and local: cheerful and thankful service is always a duty but now especially, and will give them the strength of mind and body they need both to perform what is required and to oppose the designs of their enemies. The quieting follows. Gill has the Levites make the people quiet and easy, with the governor behind them, and then go their way to eat and drink freely and cheerfully. Ellicott observes that what was said was again relayed by the Levites in various directions, against an emotion almost irrepressible, and that what the people had understood was the command to rejoice.
13:
Henry makes the second day's gathering the proof of the first day's work. They had spent most of one day praying and hearing, and the next, though no festival, the chief of them came back to hear Ezra expound, finding it more gainful than any worldly pleasure; those who understand the scriptures well, he adds, will still want to understand them better. He notices who came: the priests and Levites themselves, with the heads of the people, to be taught by that prince of expositors and so fitted to teach others. On the first day Ezra's humility had set them at his right hand and his left as fellow teachers; on the second their humility set them at his feet as learners. Wesley puts it in sharper terms: they chose to confess their ignorance rather than pretend to knowledge they had not, being more careful to learn their duty than to keep their reputation. Ellicott notes that this was the chief of the fathers and not yet the multitude, come to learn the full meaning of an almost forgotten festival, the dwelling in booths having fallen into disuse. Gill has them find it written either from the previous day's reading or in conversation with Ezra, and Clarke recalls what the feast commemorated, the sojourning in the wilderness after the deliverance from Egypt, which made its keeping the more a duty for men just out of Babylon.

The proclamation that follows is not where the sources expect it. Ellicott observes that no such command stands in the law, reports the Greek insertion naming Ezra as speaker, and prefers an emendation yielding that when they heard it they proclaimed; the order is then to gather not precisely the branches the ancient law named but such as circumstances allowed. Wesley identifies the mount as the mount of Olives, next to Jerusalem and stocked with olive and probably the other trees, which he thinks were planted there chiefly for the city's use at this feast; and he takes it as standing for any such source near the cities of Judah. Gill has the people go out to the mountains and fetch the branches in. Where the booths went is Clarke's and Ellicott's interest: Clarke reminds the reader that eastern houses have flat roofs, used for rest, for air in the heat and often for sleeping, while Ellicott adds the inner courtyards, and distinguishes those the temple ministers made from those strangers put up in the streets and open spaces by the gates.

On the closing claim every voice says how far it reaches. Ellicott hears the pathos in the title children of the captivity, and holds that though the feast had been kept in earlier reigns it had never been kept thus, with the whole people dwelling in booths. Wesley makes the difference one of manner twice over: never so joyfully, since they had not only their old causes of rejoicing but new ones, and never so religiously, since where formerly only the first and last days carried a holy convocation, the people now heard the law read every day of the feast. Clarke says plainly that no celebration since Joshua's time had been so hearty or so pious, and dismisses the legend of the sacred fire hidden in a dry well and rekindled by a sudden break of sunlight as worthy of no credit, referring the curious to the second book of Maccabees. Gill confirms the daily reading from the first day to the last, where before only the first and last had been convocations at which it seems to have been read. Delitzsch leaves the subject of that reading indefinite, though others supply Ezra, and adds two limits: the law required it only at the celebration of tabernacles falling in a sabbatical year, and the last day meant is the seventh, the eighth being a solemn assembly outside the feast.
